title: Taifas of Iberia
capsule: The taifas (Arabic: ṭawāʾif, 'faction-kingdoms') were the independent Muslim principalities that emerged across al-Andalus after the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate of Córdoba — its last caliph Hisham III deposed in 1031 — reaching a peak of over two dozen principalities including Seville, Toledo, Zaragoza, Badajoz, and Granada. Taifa rulers styled themselves as deputies of an absent caliph rather than independent kings, and their courts became major centers of Arabic poetry, philosophy, and science, including the patronage of Ibn Hazm and the poet-king al-Mu'tamid of Seville. The first taifa period ended with the Almoravid conquest of al-Andalus from 1086 onward; taifa polities recurred twice more — c. 1140–1203 after Almoravid decline and c. 1228–1248 after Almohad fragmentation — before the Reconquista eliminated all but the Emirate of Granada.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Individual taifa capitals are documented in Arabic chronicles; exact boundaries between principalities shifted frequently through warfare and dynastic succession and cannot be mapped with precision, particularly for the smaller principalities.
